grandparents.lede: Born in a farm house at Buckhorn, Oklahoma, Bob jumped out of airplanes for the U.S. Army for twenty years and came home to Choctaw County.
A Grayson County farm girl who met Bob at a skating rink, married him in 1961, raised three children on Army posts around the world, and worked forty years as a respiratory therapist.
A Winona carpenter’s son who married Diane Rivers in 1958, raised five children and became assistant superintendent of maintenance at the La Crosse YMCA.
Raised in Rollingstone, Diane graduated from Holy Trinity High School and Winona Secretarial School, raised five children and worked in La Crosse.

stories.title: Twenty years and countless jumps
stories.hook: Bob Johnson left the Oklahoma farm country, became a paratrooper, served in Vietnam and twice in Korea, and retired a Warrant Officer 3.
body: Bob Johnson spent his childhood in southeastern Oklahoma. In 1950 he was twelve and living near Hunter in Choctaw County, on the road east of Sunkist. His father Joe farmed, and the household included Joe’s wife Opal, her son Don and two young daughters. Bob’s mother, Nettie, had remarried and lived elsewhere. Opal was Nettie’s younger sister, making her both Bob’s aunt and his stepmother.

Bobby Joe Johnson was born at Buckhorn, Oklahoma, on 17 July 1937. As a young man he went to Texas, graduating from Decatur High School in 1957 and attending Decatur Baptist College before entering the Army. His later memorial places his schooling at Savoy instead; the Army hometown notices published in 1958 and 1961 give Decatur. During his youth he met Marjorie Bell at a skating rink. They married on 21 December 1961.

Bob entered the Army in February 1958 and completed basic training at Fort Ord, California. By August he had earned his parachutist wings at the 82nd Airborne Division Jump School at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. The course included five training jumps. Within months, the Buckhorn boy had gone from basic training on the Pacific coast to an airborne unit in North Carolina.

By January 1961 he was a Specialist Four serving as a supply clerk in the Mortar Battery of the 504th Infantry, 82nd Airborne Division. He had already been stationed in Germany. That month he marched with the 504th in President John F. Kennedy’s inaugural parade in Washington. His later service included one tour in Vietnam and two in Korea, although the dates of those assignments have not been established. Army life also shaped the early years of his marriage and the childhoods of his three children.

After "twenty years and countless jumps," he retired as a Warrant Officer 3 and returned to Oklahoma. A warrant officer is a technical specialist, usually promoted from the enlisted ranks after years of experience, a long way from the Buckhorn farm boy who left for the Army. In retirement he read military biographies, watched westerns, and kept his yard and vehicles immaculate. His family remembered the uniform of civilian life: button-up shirts rolled to the elbows, starched jeans, cowboy boots and one of his many Airborne hats. A daily request to Margie was whether they could go and get the grandkids.

Bob and Margie raised Joey, David and Leatha. They lost David in a highway crash in October 1988, when he was twenty-four. Bob died on 28 September 2024, aged eighty-seven, and was buried at Restland Cemetery in Boswell. His father Joe, a World War II veteran, and his son David are also buried there. After an Army career that had taken him far from home, Bob’s life ended in the southeastern Oklahoma community he loved.

quotes.t: He became a paratrooper, and after twenty years and countless jumps, Bob retired from the US Army as a Warrant Officer 3 and returned to the place he loved most, Oklahoma.

stories.title: Forty years of helping people breathe
stories.hook: Margie Bell met Bob Johnson at a Texas skating rink, followed his Army career for twenty years, then spent four decades at the bedside of patients who could not catch their breath.
body: Marjorie Ann Bell grew up in a Grayson County, Texas, farm family with two sisters, Sylvia “Sue” and June, and a brother, Glenn “Sonny.” Born on 16 March 1943 to Wayne and Melba Bell, she was seven when the 1950 census placed the family together on the farm. Basketball and skating were among her favorite pastimes. At a skating rink in her teens, she met Bobby Johnson, the young Oklahoman she would marry.

Margie graduated from S&S Consolidated High School in 1961 and began studying nursing in college. On 21 December that year she married Bob and paused her studies to join him during his Army career. They raised three children, Joey, David and Leatha, while military assignments took the family across the United States and overseas. David was born in Christian County, Kentucky, in 1964. With each move, Margie made another home for the family.

She later returned to her education and qualified as a respiratory therapist. Her career lasted forty years, and she also worked as an emergency medical technician. The nursing student who had interrupted college became a health professional with decades of practical experience caring for patients. Her family remembered the smile she brought to that work.

After Bob retired from the Army, they settled in southeastern Oklahoma. Cooking was one of the ways Margie cared for her family. She worked without a cookbook, making homemade ice cream, German chocolate cake, fried chicken and pot roast that became regular family requests. Visitors went home with leftovers. Her children and, later, grandchildren knew her table as a place where they would be fed.

Her attention extended to the flower beds. As she watered, she would say the flowers needed “a good drink.” Church and hymn singing were part of her life, and a piece of Extra gum was a familiar small offering to the people around her. These everyday details belong alongside the moves, the children and the long healthcare career in the family’s memory of Margie.

The family lost David in an October 1988 highway crash, when he was twenty-four. Margie and Bob remained married for sixty-two years, until his death in September 2024. She died at Calera, Oklahoma, on 12 February 2025, aged eighty-one. Her memorial service was held at First Baptist Church in Boswell on 17 February.

stories.title: David Glenn Johnson, 1964–1988
stories.hook: An Army childhood, school sports in Boswell and a life remembered by the Johnson family.
body: David Glenn Johnson had been born on 8 July 1964 in Christian County, Kentucky, the county that holds Fort Campbell, while his father Bob was a career paratrooper. He was the middle child between Joey and Leatha. He grew up in the Army's moves and then in Boswell, and the school portraits in the family's collection show a long-haired boy in the class pictures, a basketball player in number 21, and a ballplayer at the plate.

The family’s photographs preserve David at several stages of childhood: in school portraits, on the basketball court wearing number 21, and at the plate with a bat. They offer a view of the boy and young man beyond the newspaper account of his death.

At about 7:35 on the evening of Wednesday, 19 October 1988, an Oklahoma Highway Patrol lieutenant was driving east on Highway 3, seven miles east of Atoka, when he clocked an oncoming 1980 Chevrolet pickup at 96 miles an hour. By the time he turned around the driver had lost control on a curve. The pickup rolled at least five times and came to rest on its side beside a fence line. The rear bumper seemed to have caught a tree, spinning the truck and tearing the tires off the rims. Both men inside had been thrown out: the driver, twenty-one, of Bennington, and his passenger, David Johnson of Boswell.

The Lane First Responders and two ambulances took them to Atoka Memorial Hospital. David was moved on to Texoma Medical Center in Denison, Texas, where he died at about 3 a.m. on Thursday, 20 October, of head and internal injuries. He was twenty-four. The trooper said alcohol was involved and that neither man wore a seat belt. The driver was charged with manslaughter on Friday.

David was buried at Restland Cemetery in Boswell, where his grandfather Joe Johnson had been buried in 1972. His parents, Bob and Margie, and his brother and sister survived him. When Bob died in 2024, thirty-six years later, David remained among the family members remembered before him.

stories.title: Joe Johnson of the Boehler route
stories.hook: A Soper-born stockman who built airfields in World War II and married two Tyson sisters, one after the other.
body: On 16 October 1940, a few weeks before the first peacetime draft numbers were drawn, Joel Gilbert Johnson filled out his registration card at Boehler, Oklahoma. He was thirty-two, self-employed, five feet eight, 180 pounds, with a ruddy complexion, black hair and brown eyes. For the person who would always know where to find him he gave his father, Joel.

Everyone called him Joe. He had been born at Soper in Choctaw County on 24 July 1908, the year after Oklahoma became a state, to Joel A. Johnson and Winnie Bozarth. Soper itself was barely six. It had sprung up in 1902 when the Arkansas and Choctaw Railway ran a line through southern Choctaw County, and it was named for the railroad's attorney. Joe grew up in the cotton, corn and cattle economy of that railroad country, and by 1930, at twenty-one, he was living at home in Boswell. His father was buying stock for a living.

Joe married Nettie Beatrice Tyson, and their son Bobby was born in 1937. In April 1940 the census taker found Nettie, twenty-six, and "Bobbin J.," two, at her father Albert Tyson's rented farm at Oakes, while Joe was at Boehler with his own father. The marriage did not last. Nettie later married Bob Tillery. By 1950 Joe was farming on the road east of Sunkist, near Hunter, and his wife was Opal, Nettie's younger sister, whose first husband had been a Wilson. Bob lived with them. Their story is told in the sisters' own.

The war interrupted. Joe enlisted on 25 May 1942, at thirty-three, and served until 21 October 1945 as a Technician Fifth Grade in the 872nd Engineer Aviation Battalion. Engineer aviation battalions were built to build airfields: each was organized to put in an advanced airdrome on its own, with runways, taxiways and the roads and buildings around them. The Army fielded 157 of them, and by war's end aviation engineers had built or improved more than a thousand airfields around the world.

Joe returned to the Boehler route and to work with cattle. He belonged to the American Legion at Boswell and was remembered as a former stockman. He died early on 25 November 1972, aged sixty-four, following an apparent heart attack. His funeral was held at the Church of Christ in Boswell, with burial at Restland Cemetery. His military headstone commemorates his service in the 872nd Engineer Aviation Battalion. His son Bob was then in the middle of his own Army career.

stories.title: Two sisters under one roof in 1940
stories.hook: In April 1940 the census taker found Nettie and Opal Tyson, both young mothers, back at their father's farm at Oakes. Ten years later Opal was married to Nettie's former husband.
body: That April the enumerator called at the rented farm of Albert Tyson at Oakes, in Choctaw County. Albert was sixty-five, born in Texas, schooled through the third grade, and farming on his own account. With him were his wife Elizabeth, fifty-nine, and their son Marion, seventeen. Also in the house were two grown daughters and their babies: Nettie Johnson, twenty-six, with her two-year-old son, written down as "Bobbin J. Johnson"; and Opal Wilson, twenty-one, with an infant son, Don.

The county was cotton, corn and hay country in the Depression years. Two married daughters and two grandchildren back under the parents' roof was not unusual. Nettie's husband Joe Johnson was not in the house; that October he was at Boehler with his own father. Opal had married in July 1938, at eighteen: "Seidel Wilson to Opal Tyson, Boswell."

A decade later the household had rearranged itself. In 1950 Joe Johnson was farming on the road east of Sunkist, near Hunter, with Opal as his wife. In the house were Bob, twelve, Opal's son Don, ten, listed as Joe's stepson, and two little daughters. The Arkansas marriage record in Sevier County shows Joel Gilbert Johnson, sixty, marrying Opal Wilson on 3 December 1968; she was "the former Opal Tyson." Nettie, meanwhile, married Bob Tillery, and their son Y. Q. Tillery, born at Boswell in 1942, became Bob's half-brother.

Nettie was Bob’s mother; Opal was his aunt and later his stepmother. The family’s relationships are easy to blur when both sisters appear in different Johnson households. Nettie appears in Bob’s Army hometown notices as Mrs. Nettie B. McCarter of Sherman in 1958 and Mrs. Nettie B. Tillery of Sadler in 1961. She died on 6 February 1980 and is buried at Sunnyside Cemetery in Savoy, Texas. Bob’s extended household included his half-brother Y. Q. Tillery, stepbrother Don Wilson and sisters Kay and Sue. The distinctions explain the family’s connections without making Opal his birth mother.

stories.title: Wayne and Melba Bell’s Grayson County family
stories.hook: Wayne Bell and Melba Williams married in 1937 and raised the Texas farm family in which Margie grew up.
body: Wayne Douglas Bell and Melba Nena Williams were married at Van Alstyne, Texas, on 18 September 1937. He was twenty-three, born at Anna in Collin County on 18 April 1914, the son of Charles Hercules "Lee" Bell and Mary Alice Baker. She was nineteen, born at Van Alstyne on 13 March 1918, the daughter of Cleave and Willie (Parker) Williams. Both had grown up within a few miles of Mantua, the seminary town that had died when the railroad missed it in 1872, and of the two railroad towns that replaced it.

They married in the Depression, when farming in the Blackland country was shrinking. Collin County lost more than 1,200 farms between 1930 and 1940, and Grayson County nearly 900. In 1940 the Bells were renters on Worchester Road in Grayson County, with their first baby, a daughter. Wayne was twenty-six, five feet ten, 175 pounds, with brown hair and gray eyes; when he registered for the draft that October he was working for Kimble Farms Inc.

By 1950 the family had grown to four children: Sue, eleven; Margie, seven, Rachel's grandmother; Glenn, four; and Norma June, two. The census taker wrote the youngest two as "Scharffer," but the family knew them as Glenn "Sonny" and June. In 1954 the Bells were on Route 1 near Collinsville. On 9 April Melba gave birth prematurely at St. Vincent's Hospital in Sherman to a son. He lived seven hours. The death certificate, signed by Dr. H. L. Brown, gives the cause as pulmonary edema due to premature birth, and Wayne signed as informant. The baby was buried the next day in West Hill Cemetery, Sherman. Margie was eleven.

Wayne came from a large family. When one of his sisters died in 1968, four sisters and four brothers were still living: Ora Bell Russell, Mrs. J. R. Chapman, Mrs. Cecil Field and Mrs. S. W. Turner, and Charlie of Van Alstyne, Wayne of Denison, Jack of Galesburg, Illinois, and Hardy of Anna.

Melba belonged to Cherry Mound Baptist Church. She died at home in Denison on 22 September 1981, aged sixty-three, and was buried at Van Alstyne. Wayne lived until 22 July 1991. Their daughter Margie carried the Bell family into another chapter: she married Bob Johnson in 1961, raised three children through Army moves and eventually settled in southeastern Oklahoma.

stories.title: Sixty years of buying cattle in Choctaw County
stories.hook: Born in Milam County, Texas, in 1875, Joel Anderson Johnson came to Choctaw County around 1900 and was still called a rancher when he died in 1961.
body: In 1930 the census taker at Boswell, Oklahoma, wrote down Joel Johnson's trade as stock buyer, and his employer as a cattle compress. He was fifty-five. In a county where the land ran to cattle, hay and cotton, a stock buyer was the man who bought animals from farmers and sold them on, and the work depended on knowing every farm, fence and creditor for miles around. He owned his house. His son Joel Gilbert, twenty-one, and a granddaughter, Lila Smith, lived with him and his wife Winnie.

He had been born on 2 April 1875 in Milam County, Texas, cotton and ranch country east of Austin, where most of the settlers had come from the South. His father was born in Arkansas and his mother in Mississippi. In 1896 he married Winnie Bozarth in Texas. A few years later the couple crossed the Red River into the Choctaw Nation, and he lived in the community sixty years, which puts the move at about 1900. Soper and Boswell had both started in 1902, the year the Arkansas and Choctaw Railway came through, so the family arrived just as the towns did.

By 1910, three years after statehood, the Johnsons were in Oakes township with five children: Aletha, twelve; Porter, nine; George, six; Willie, four; and Joel, one, the future Joe who would father Bob. The county then raised mainly cotton. By 1930 it had diversified into corn, oats, prairie hay and peanuts, which suited a man who dealt in stock. In 1940 Joel and Winnie were farming on the road to Sunkist in Hunter township, and in October of that year their son Joe named him on a draft card as the person who would always know where to find him.

Joel died on a Wednesday night in March 1961 at Memorial Hospital in Hugo. He was eighty-five. He was a "retired farmer and rancher," a resident of the community for sixty years and a member of the Church of Christ. He was buried at Restland Cemetery. He was survived by his wife Winnie, sons G. F. Johnson of Soper and Joe G. Johnson of Boswell, a daughter in Sterling, Texas, two brothers in California and Colorado, and three sisters in Hugo, Soper and Byars, Texas. It is the picture of a family that came north from Texas together and scattered only a little.

stories.title: A reception for 350 on the Rivers lawn
stories.hook: On a July morning in 1958 an eighteen-year-old from a Luxembourg village married a Winona carpenter's son, and half of Rollingstone ended up on her father's lawn.
body: The Saturday began early. At 9:30 on the morning of 26 July 1958, Diane Rivers, eighteen, walked up the aisle of Holy Trinity Catholic Church in Rollingstone, Minnesota, to marry David Nelton, nineteen. The Rev. George Moudry performed the double-ring ceremony and celebrated the nuptial Mass, and the altars were banked with pink and white gladioli and lighted candles. Her father, Edward, gave her away.

Her dress was Chantilly lace and tulle over bridal satin, with a lace bodice, long sleeves, a sabrina neckline, a full floor-length skirt, and a veil of silk illusion falling from a lace cap. She carried a cascade of white roses and a double orchid. The pearl necklace and bracelet were David's gift.

Diane’s sister Mary Lynn was maid of honor. Angela Rivers played the organ, Uncle Paul Rivers ushered and cousins served the Mass. Douglas Trainor of Winona was David’s best man, and his sister Sandra was a bridesmaid. The ceremony brought the family into Holy Trinity’s limestone church, built in 1869 with parishioners supplying labor and money and enlarged in 1893. It was a familiar center of life for the Rivers and Frisch families.

After a wedding dinner in the Flamingo Room of the Hotel Winona, a reception for 350 guests was held on the lawn of Edward and Viola Rivers’s home. Edward sold insurance in Rollingstone, where Viola had lived throughout their marriage. The couple’s families had deep local roots: earlier Rivers generations had run the post office and carried rural mail, while Viola’s Frisch relatives farmed at Oak Ridge.

The two families came from different sides of the same county. The Riverses and Frisches were Luxembourg Catholics who had settled the hills west of Winona in the 1850s and 1860s. The Neltons were Germans in town: George Nelton, David's grandfather, was a Winona house carpenter who became a contractor, and David himself was a Winona Senior High graduate who had spent time at Winona State College and now worked for his father, Arthur, a carpenter. Diane had finished Holy Trinity High School and Winona Secretarial School. Winona was a lumber, river and railroad city whose population had long been a mix of German, Polish and Yankee families, and weddings like this one stitched the town to the villages above it.

After a trip to the Wisconsin Dells, Diane and David made their home in Minnesota City, where his parents lived. They later moved to Houston, Minnesota, and then rural Holmen, Wisconsin. Five children were born during their marriage. Their wedding photograph preserves the beginning of that family, gathered at the church and home that had anchored Diane’s childhood.

stories.title: David Nelton, carpenter’s son and father of five
stories.hook: From Winona and Minnesota City to the La Crosse YMCA, David’s life followed the Mississippi valley.
body: David John Nelton had been born in Winona on 19 July 1938, the son of Arthur and Helen (Canfield) Nelton. The 1940 census found the family renting on Lake Park Boulevard in Winona; by 1950 they were in Minnesota City, where his father worked as a carpenter in building construction. He graduated from Winona Senior High, worked for his father the carpenter, and in 1958 married Diane Rivers at Rollingstone.

The couple lived in Minnesota City and then Houston, Minnesota, before crossing the Mississippi to rural Holmen, Wisconsin, about 1971. They had five children. David had become assistant superintendent of maintenance at the La Crosse YMCA.

David’s working life began in the family building trade. His father Arthur and grandfather George were both carpenters, and before his 1958 marriage he worked for Arthur. His later maintenance role at the YMCA placed him in another practical occupation, caring for a building used by the wider community.

At 2:44 a.m. on Saturday 12 February 1977, David Nelton was driving north on Highway 53 near the George Street intersection in La Crosse, Wisconsin, when his car and a southbound pickup truck collided head-on in the south lane. He was taken to Lutheran Hospital and died there at 3:13. His death and five others that weekend brought Wisconsin's 1977 traffic toll to eighty.

His funeral was at St. Paul's Catholic Church in Minnesota City, with a Rosary at Fawcett Funeral Home in Winona the night before. The Rev. Joseph C. Frisch officiated; the priest shares the surname of Diane's mother's family, though no relation is established. The ground was frozen, so burial at Oakwood Cemetery, Minnesota City, waited until spring. His pallbearers were Richard Hohensee, Wayne Valentine, Charles Neuman, John Brown, Hollis Donehower and Robert Rolbiecki.

David was thirty-eight. His parents Arthur and Helen survived him, as did Diane and their five children. Arthur lived until 1984 and Helen until 1982. David’s grave at Oakwood Cemetery in Minnesota City places him back in the community where he had grown up and begun married life.

stories.title: Diane Rivers Nelton: family and working life
stories.hook: Raised in Rollingstone, Diane made homes in Minnesota and Wisconsin, raised five children and worked in La Crosse.
body: Diane Mary Rivers was born in St. Paul on 10 August 1939 to Edward and Viola (Frisch) Rivers and grew up at Rollingstone, where her father sold insurance. She graduated from Holy Trinity High School and Winona Secretarial School. On 26 July 1958, aged eighteen, she married David Nelton at Holy Trinity Catholic Church. They began married life in Minnesota City and later lived in Houston, Minnesota, and rural Holmen, Wisconsin.

Diane and David had five children. Alongside family life, she worked in La Crosse. After E.T.C. Inc. dismissed her in January 1975, she filed a sex-discrimination complaint with Wisconsin’s labor department. By December 1976 the complaint had been dismissed after the hearing examiner found no evidence that the dismissal was based on sex. The complaint and its outcome are documented in a contemporary La Crosse newspaper report.

Her mother Viola died in August 1975. In February 1977 David died after a head-on collision in La Crosse, leaving Diane widowed at thirty-seven. On 28 May 1977 she married Stephen Lee Fascher, a sales manager at La Crosse Glass Co. and a National Guard member from Farmersburg, Iowa. The family lived at Bangor. Stephen died at Lutheran Hospital on 7 August 1978, aged thirty-one; the cause had not been determined when the notice was published.

Her father, Edward, died in January 1980. On 13 August 1983 Diane married Charles Antony in La Crosse and they lived at Bangor. She worked at Hillview Nursing Home until December 1986. Diane M. Antony died of cancer at St. Francis Medical Center on Friday 27 March 1987, at forty-seven, and after a funeral at St. Peter's Catholic Church in Middle Ridge she was buried in St. Mary's Catholic Cemetery at Bangor.

Diane’s family remained connected to the Rollingstone generations before her. Her mother Viola had been only sixteen months old when her own mother, Maggie Frisch, died in 1906. Diane’s five children belonged to that continuing Rivers and Frisch family as well as to the Nelton and Canfield branches along the Mississippi.

stories.title: Arthur Nelton, carpenter and fireman
stories.hook: Arthur Nelton framed houses around Winona through the Depression and after, sat on the Minnesota City council, fought fires as a volunteer, and outlived his only son.
body: Arthur Nelton was a carpenter in a family of carpenters. In 1940 he and Helen rented a home on Lake Park Boulevard in Winona, with their small son David. Arthur was thirty, had completed a year of college and reported annual earnings of $1,800. His father George was a local contractor, and Arthur and his brother Irwin worked in the family firm.

Arthur R. Nelton had been born in Winona on 27 October 1909, one of four children of George Nelton and Anna Brose, both of German background, and his father was already a house carpenter working his way toward a contracting firm. His mother died in April 1928, when he was eighteen. When George later organized his own firm, his sons Arthur and Irwin joined him in it.

On 15 August 1934, with the building trades still near their lowest point, he married Helen Canfield in Winona. She had been born on 9 November 1910 at Kellogg, in Wabasha County, to James and Nel (Heffernan) Canfield. Her father died at Wabasha on 19 June 1912, when she was nineteen months old. After the wedding she kept house in Minnesota City for most of her life and belonged to St. Paul's Catholic Church there.

By 1950 Arthur and Helen lived in Minnesota City with David and their daughter Sandra. Arthur continued as a self-employed building carpenter in the Winona area until retiring in 1979. He belonged to Carpenters Union Local 307, served on the Minnesota City council and volunteered with the local fire department. His work and public service both kept him closely involved in the community. David worked for him before marrying Diane Rivers in 1958.

Helen died at home on 30 November 1982, aged seventy-two, and her grandsons Dirk and Kendrick carried her coffin. Two years later, on 7 October 1984, Arthur died at Lutheran Hospital in La Crosse, the same hospital where his son David had died in 1977. He was seventy-four. Dirk and Kendrick were his pallbearers too. He had spent his working life putting up other families' houses; in the last seven years of his life he buried his only son and then his wife.

quotes.t: He was a member of the Carpenters Union, Local 307, a past member of the Minnesota City Council and a past member of the Minnesota City Volunteer Fire Department.

stories.title: George Nelton built Winona
stories.hook: George Nelton framed Winona houses for four decades, went south to the Florida boom for two winters, and was working until three months before he died.
body: George Nelton "built many of the homes in the city and some of the early stores, and also remodeled some of the Winona store fronts." He had gone on working until 1 August 1952; one of the last houses he finished was the Arthur Tarras home in Glen Mary. Three months later, on 12 November, he died at Winona General Hospital at seventy after a long illness.

George John Nelton was born in Winona on 17 January 1882 to German-born George Nelton and Eda Zenk. Winona remained his home throughout his life, although contracting work sometimes took him elsewhere. The river city’s houses, businesses and changing storefronts became the setting for his long building career.

The 1910 census finds him at 617 West King Street, twenty-eight years old, a house carpenter renting with his wife Anna (Brose) and four small children: Myrtle, Irwin, Edward and the baby, Arthur, who was Rachel's great-grandfather. His father is said to have died the year after, on 19 October 1911. George worked as a carpenter, then for the contracting firm of Hanson & Nelton, and finally organized a firm of his own, in which his sons Arthur and Irwin worked.

In the winters of 1924 and 1925 he went to Florida and took contracting work there. Those were the peak years of the Florida land boom, when Northern money and Northern builders poured into Miami and the new planned towns around it, and when the shortage of building supplies grew so bad that the railroads put an embargo on freight in October 1925. Within a year the boom was over, and the 1926 Miami hurricane finished it. A Winona contractor went south twice and came home.

Anna died in April 1928, when Arthur was eighteen. In 1930 George married Christine Walstad, a Norwegian immigrant who had come to America in 1904, and the second marriage brought three stepsons, three stepdaughters and nine step-grandchildren into the family. He was a member of the Eagles Club and of the Winona Contractors Association, and "an enthusiastic fisherman."

George was buried at Woodlawn Cemetery. Ernest Brose was among his pallbearers, linking the funeral to Anna’s family. His sons Arthur and Irwin continued the family’s connection with carpentry. Through Arthur and his son David, George’s building trade became part of the story of three Nelton generations.

stories.title: The Rivers family of Rollingstone
stories.hook: Edward Rivers sold insurance from the village where he was born and buried; Viola, who lost her mother at sixteen months, lived there all her married life.
body: Edward Nicholas Rivers was born at Rollingstone on 20 October 1910, the eldest of nine children of Edward Rivers and Johanna Johns, and he did not leave. On 14 June 1933, at Rollingstone, he married Viola Frisch, who had been born on 9 June 1905 at Oak Ridge, a few miles away, to John and Maggie Frisch. The wedding came in the third year of the Depression and he was twenty-two. The next March Viola's father died, and that same year Edward began as an insurance agent in the village.

Insurance ran in the village. His own father had carried the rural mail out of Rollingstone for thirty years, and Viola's father had been secretary of the Rollingstone Mutual Fire Insurance company for twenty-four. Edward would sit on that company's board and serve as president of the Rollingstone Business Association and of the St. Nicholas Society, the parish society his father had belonged to before him. He was also a Knight of Columbus and an Elk.

Their daughters were Diane, born in St. Paul on 10 August 1939, and Mary Lynn. In the Rivers house the family was never small: when Diane married in 1958 the cousins served the Mass and an uncle ushered, and 350 people ate on the lawn. Viola belonged to Holy Trinity Church, the ladies aid and the St. Theresa Society, where she was a charter member.

Viola died on 13 August 1975, aged seventy, while on the way to St. Elizabeth’s Hospital in Wabasha. Her funeral Mass was held at Holy Trinity, and she was buried in the parish cemetery. Edward, their daughters Diane and Mary Lynn, her sister Gertrude Koetter and eight grandchildren survived her. From her 1933 marriage until her death, Rollingstone had been her home.

Edward married again in 1976, to Elizabeth "Betty" Lehnertz Greden, who died in 1977. He died at home in Rollingstone on 14 January 1980, after an illness of several months, and his brothers Bernard, Norbert, Arthur and Paul carried him to the cemetery. His brother Francis died on 22 November 1944 at the age of seventeen.

stories.title: A horse, a prison, and Cleave Williams's brother
stories.hook: Melba Bell's father farmed at Van Alstyne. His youngest brother went to the state prison at seventeen for stealing a horse and was dead at twenty.
body: George Williams was born near Mantua, Texas, on 1 February 1891, the youngest child of Thomas and Rebecca Williams. A family account tells of his arrest at seventeen with John Leo Skipworth for stealing a horse and of a prison term at Huntsville. In the story passed down through the family, George had found another caller visiting a girl, taken the other man’s horse and ridden it to death. This account is family tradition; the underlying court and prison records have not been checked.

The same account relates that George developed diabetes in prison, was released and died a few weeks later with his parents beside him. He died on 31 May 1911, aged twenty, and was buried at Van Alstyne. His death certificate describes him as married, which conflicts with the family account. That discrepancy remains unresolved.

His brother Grover Cleveland "Cleave" Williams was four years older, born in 1887 in Tennessee, the farm country around the old Shiloh battlefield, before Thomas and Rebecca brought the family to Texas about 1891. Thomas, born 9 February 1847, and Rebecca, born 14 February 1850, lie in Van Alstyne Cemetery; their stone gives his death as 25 December 1933 and hers as 20 September 1927.

Willie Parker was born in Texas on 13 January 1891 to James and Amanda (Pipkin) Parker. She and Cleave married and farmed near Van Alstyne. Their daughter Melba was born there in 1918 and married Wayne Bell in 1937. Through Melba and her daughter Margie, the Williams and Parker families connect to Rachel’s Johnson branch.

Cleave died on 5 December 1949. Willie lived another twenty-five years, a member of the Van Alstyne First Methodist Church, and died in a Sherman hospital on the morning of 18 November 1974, aged eighty-three. Their daughter Melba's family would grow into the Bell farm story told elsewhere on this site. Cleave and Willie are buried at Van Alstyne.

stories.title: The Canfields of Canfield Springs
stories.hook: In the summer of 1855 a Pennsylvania farmer built a small house in Cook's Valley, Minnesota, and four generations later his great-granddaughter married a Winona carpenter.
body: John and Margaret (Greer) Canfield brought their family from Pennsylvania to Wabasha County, Minnesota, in 1855. John and Patrick McDonough were among the earliest Euro-American settlers in Highland Township. The Canfields settled in the upper part of Cook’s Valley, at the place that became known as Canfield Springs. Their move was part of the settlement of Dakota homelands following the contested land cessions of the 1850s.

John Canfield was a community man. On 8 November 1857 the neighbors met in G. A. Cook's house to organize a school district, and named him director. The first road in the township, laid out in 1858, ran between Appel's Mill and Canfield Springs. The couple farmed there for the rest of their lives and raised ten children. Margaret is said to have died in 1865 at Kellogg.

Their son John A. Canfield was born in Pennsylvania on 29 June 1848 and came to Highland as a boy of seven. He settled at Kellogg and married Anna Hall, the only daughter of George W. Hall, a Pennsylvania-born furniture dealer who had moved from Iowa to Wabasha in 1857. Their marriage is placed at 1875 in the family tree, although the marriage record has not been verified. Anna was born 18 August 1855 in Iowa, so she would have been twenty. She bore a son, James Garfield Canfield, in September 1881, and died at Kellogg on 24 February 1882, five months later.

Anna Hall’s parents added another Wabasha connection. Her father George W. Hall, born in Perry County, Pennsylvania, in 1824, moved into the grocery trade at Muscatine, Iowa, in 1854. He and his wife Sarah came to Wabasha in 1857, where he opened a furniture store with her brother Samuel Butturff. A three-year attempt at farming in Glasgow Township began in 1860, but poor health brought him back to town. He later worked as a store clerk and kept a meat market. When he died in 1870, he owned two adjoining houses on Allegheny Street.

James grew up to marry Helen "Nel" Heffernan and lived at Kellogg, where their daughter Helen was born on 9 November 1910. He died at Wabasha on 19 June 1912, aged thirty. He is buried at St. Agnes Cemetery in Kellogg. His brothers and sisters included George (called Duke), John Wilson, Anna Flint, Walter, Homer, Edith, Margaret Bayer, Ruth, Elmer and Beryl Rock. Helen was his only child.

The thread between this farm and the Neltons runs through two lost parents. James's mother died when he was an infant, and Helen's father died when she was a toddler. Helen, Rachel's great-grandmother, married Arthur Nelton in Winona on 15 August 1934. Nel's parents and her later life are not established.

quotes.t: Patrick McDonough and John Canfield were the first settlers of this town. They came in the summer of 1855 and built small homes for themselves, installed their families therein, and went to work.

stories.title: The year the railroad came to Choctaw County
stories.hook: In 1902 the Arkansas and Choctaw Railway laid track through southern Choctaw County, and two towns the Johnsons and Tysons would live in either began or moved to meet it.
body: By 1901 Mayhew, in the Choctaw Nation, was down to an estimated twenty-nine people, one cotton gin and one general store. It had once been the capital of the Pushmataha District, with a Presbyterian mission school from 1839 and a court ground, but the Curtis Act of 1898 had abolished the tribal governments, and its reason for being went with them. Then in 1902 the Arkansas and Choctaw Railway ran its line about two miles south. The businesses and families moved to the tracks. In September the post office became Boswell, named for Amity V. Boswell, who had surveyed the right-of-way.

The same railway helped establish Soper in 1902. Named for the line’s attorney, Pliny L. Soper, the town opened its post office in April 1903. A Methodist congregation organized in 1904 and the Soper Herald began publishing by January 1907. At Oklahoma statehood in 1907 Soper had 296 residents; by 1920 it had 538, with two doctors, two banks, four churches, a newspaper and three cotton gins. Boswell grew from 836 at statehood to 1,212 in 1920, shipping cotton, corn and fruit from its depot.

Rachel's Johnson and Tyson families belonged to this new country. Joel A. Johnson crossed from Texas about 1900 and bought and sold cattle for the next sixty years. His son Joe was born at Soper in 1908, the year after statehood. Nettie and Opal Tyson were in Albert Tyson's rented farmhouse at Oakes in 1940, and Opal had been born in 1919 at Sand Bluff. Joe died at home on the Boehler route near Boswell in 1972. His son Bob, after twenty years in the Army, retired to Oklahoma and was buried at Restland Cemetery in Boswell in 2024, near his own son David, killed in 1988 at twenty-four.

The railroad towns did not last at their peaks. Boswell stayed a farm town, but Soper shrank from 481 people in 1940 to 322 in 1970. In 1960 a tornado destroyed most of its brick downtown. By 1990 the cotton fields had become pasture, and the town was down to about 300.

Compare the Texas side of the family. The Williams and Bell ancestors farmed Grayson and Collin counties, where another railroad, the Houston and Texas Central, had killed one town (Mantua) and made two more (Van Alstyne and Anna) about thirty years earlier. Bob and Margie's families each grew up beside a railroad's route, one on each side of the Red River.

stories.title: The Vice President question
stories.hook: Rachel's tree runs the Johnsons back to Great Crossing, Kentucky, and the family of Vice President Richard M. Johnson. No record has yet proved the one link that matters.
body: Great Crossing, in Scott County, Kentucky, was the home of Col. Robert Johnson (1745-1815) and Jemima Suggett, who raised eleven children. One of them, Richard Mentor Johnson, became Vice President of the United States, serving from 1837 to 1841. Another, Joel Johnson (1790-1846), married Verlinda Offutt in 1817, founded Lakeport Plantation on Lake Chicot in Arkansas about 1831, and is buried in Frankfort Cemetery beside his brother Richard.

Rachel's online tree runs a line from this family to George Washington Johnson, born in Mississippi in 1851 and dead at Soper, Oklahoma, in 1932. The path would go through a son of Joel's named Jonathan T. Johnson (1824-1859). The geography is plausible, because Lake Chicot in Chicot County, Arkansas, sits across the Mississippi from the Delta counties of Mississippi.

The records do not back it up. The Lakeport children are Lycurgus, Julia, Betsy and Cyrus, and none is a Jonathan. Joel did have a brother, John Telemachus Johnson (1788-1856), and the name may have got scrambled in a copied tree. Nothing so far links George Washington Johnson to Kentucky at all, and the nearest record the tree offers is that a son was born in Texas about 1875, and the Fail family of George's wife Marjorie were in Milam County, Texas, by 1870.

For now this is a family story with a famous name attached, not a fact. The Scottish noble ancestry further up the same branch, the Earls of Annandale, is a well-known copied-tree error and should not be repeated.

stories.title: Rollingstone: a Luxembourg village on the Rolling Stone creek
stories.hook: A utopian colony failed at the mouth of a creek, and a few miles up the valley farmers from Luxembourg built a limestone church that still anchors the village where Diane Rivers was married.
body: Rollingstone developed inland from the Mississippi, near the meeting of the north and west branches of Rolling Stone Creek. Minnesota City had been laid out nearer the river in 1852 by the Western Farm and Village Association, a colony organized in New York. Luxembourg immigrants began settling the surrounding hills in the 1850s. Their farms, parish and businesses gave Rollingstone a distinct community life within the same township.

Among the immigrants were Michael and Margaret Rivers, who reached America in 1854 and settled on a Winona County farm in 1855. The Frisch family followed in 1864 or 1865, making their home at Oak Ridge. The two families belonged to a larger Luxembourg community whose ties continued through marriage, farming, local businesses and the Catholic parish.

By 1883 Rollingstone had three stores, two hotels, two blacksmith shops, a stone Catholic church and parsonage, a schoolhouse and several saloons. The church served much of the surrounding population. This was the village in which the Rivers family carried mail, kept stores and later sold insurance, while the Frisches farmed nearby.

Holy Trinity Church was built in 1869 under Charles Wender from rough-cut limestone, originally measuring 35 by 60 feet. Parishioners supplied labor and financial support. A transept and chancel added in 1893 under local carpenter Nicholas Arnoldy doubled the seating. A grade school opened in 1886, followed by a new school and the community’s first high school in 1921. Edward N. Rivers was among its graduates. The church was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1984.

For the families in this history the church marks every turning point. John Frisch's funeral in 1934, Viola Frisch Rivers's in 1975 and Edward N. Rivers's in 1980 were held at Holy Trinity, and Diane Rivers and David Nelton were married there in 1958. Parish societies carried the social life: Edward Rivers Sr. and his son Edward both belonged to the St. Nicholas Society, and Edward Jr. served sixteen years as its president, while Viola was a charter member of the St. Theresa Society. The village also sustained its own Rollingstone Mutual Fire Insurance company. The local historian Mary E. Nilles wrote the standard account, Rollingstone: A Luxembourgish Village in Minnesota (1983), which the nomination cites.

The family also belonged to Winona and Minnesota City down the valley. The Neltons worked in carpentry and building, while the Brose siblings belonged to several different churches. Diane Rivers and David Nelton’s 1958 wedding brought these town and village branches together at Holy Trinity. Their reception on the Rivers lawn was both a family celebration and part of Rollingstone’s continuing social life.

quotes.t: In 1855, the first German settlers from Luxembourg arrived in the rolling hills of Winona County. Bringing with them their strong Catholic religious heritage, the immigrants had, by 1861, established a cemetery and built a church.

stories.title: The Rivers family: from Heffingen to the Rollingstone post office
stories.hook: Michel Rivers brought his children from Luxembourg in 1854; two sons and a grandson kept Rollingstone's mail moving for most of the next eighty years.
body: In February 1903 the Post Office opened a new rural route out of Rollingstone, and Edward Rivers, aged twenty-one, was named its carrier. Rural Free Delivery was new; Congress had mandated it in 1893, but it did not spread across the country until about 1902, and until then a farm family had to fetch its mail from the nearest post office or pay a private carrier. Edward kept the route for thirty years and retired on 1 March 1934. His father, Henry, had held the Rollingstone post office until his death in 1886.

Michel Rivers and Margaretha Adehm left Luxembourg in 1854 and settled on a Winona County farm in 1855. Their son Henry had been born at Heffingen, in the canton of Mersch, on 11 April 1838. The move placed the family among the Luxembourg immigrants who formed a lasting community around Rollingstone. American records use the surname Rivers; an earlier Luxembourg form of the name has not been established.

John Baptiste Rivers, born in Luxembourg on 16 June 1840, made the family's public name. In March 1865 he enlisted in Co. K of the 48th Wisconsin Volunteer Infantry, a regiment organized that spring and sent to the Kansas frontier, and he served at Fort Lyon, Colorado, 'protecting the frontier against the Indians.' After the war he farmed in Norton township, and in 1872 opened a store in Rollingstone village. He was postmaster for 27 years, first president of the village council and a founder of the First State Bank of Rollingstone. The post office history reads: 'In 1886, J. B. Rivers succeeded Hy. Rivers.' Henry, his brother, had held the office and died on 10 June 1886.

Henry's widow Elizabeth Lehnertz, born in Luxembourg in 1847, had come over in 1860. After Henry's death the family ran a hotel in the village. Their son Edward, born at Rollingstone on 4 November 1881, went to the parochial school, carried the rural mail, helped found the Rollingstone Co-operative Oil Association, sold insurance for Farmers Home Mutual and served as mayor from 1938 to 1948. On 22 June 1909 he married Johanna Johns, and nine children followed. The first, Edward Nicholas, was born on 20 October 1910.

Edward N. Rivers went into insurance at Rollingstone in 1934, the year after he married Viola Frisch, and died at home on 14 January 1980. His brother Francis, born 1927, died on 22 November 1944, aged seventeen. The families were already tied before Edward and Viola married: Viola's aunt Katherine Frisch had married Matthew Rivers, a son of John B., on 19 November 1907, and the couple ran a grocery in Rollingstone. 'Mrs. Mathew Rivers, Rollingstone' was among John Frisch's sisters at his death in 1934.

quotes.t: John B. Rivers was born in Luxemburg, June 16, 1840, son of Michael and Margaret (Adam) Rivers, who came to America in 1854, and settled on a farm in Winona county in 1855.

stories.title: Oak Ridge, autumn 1906: two funerals in three weeks
stories.hook: Viola Frisch was sixteen months old when her mother died fourteen days after giving birth, and nineteen days later her grandfather, the Luxembourg pioneer, was dead as well.
body: Maggie (Haines) Frisch died at home on Oak Ridge on the evening of 1 October 1906, her fifth wedding anniversary. She was thirty-one. She and John P. Frisch had three young children: Gertrude, about three; Viola, sixteen months; and a baby only fourteen days old. Maggie’s funeral was held that Thursday at the Oak Ridge Catholic church. John, a former schoolteacher, was left to raise the children on the family farm.

Nineteen days later, on Saturday 20 October, John's father died of diabetes at sixty-nine. In 1906 there was no treatment for it; insulin was not isolated until 1921. Jacques, or Jacob, Frisch, had been born at Beaufort in the canton of Echternach on 28 October 1837, and he was 'one of the old settlers and highly esteemed citizens of Winona county,' survived by 'John, whose wife died two weeks ago.'

Jacques and Anna (Speltz) Frisch had emigrated from Luxembourg and settled at Oak Ridge. Anna was born at Fischbach on 24 October 1836. Their arrival at Winona is remembered as 4 July, although their memorial notices differ on the year: Anna’s gives 1864 and Jacques’s gives 1865. Jacob helped establish the Oak Ridge Catholic congregation, organized at John Speltz’s house on 5 December 1875. Anna died on 7 May 1902 after nearly a year of illness.

So within four years the Oak Ridge farm lost Anna, who had come from Luxembourg, then Maggie, who had married into the family, and then Jacques. John P. Frisch, born 25 July 1873, had taught school for eight years before he married Maggie Haines of Arcadia, Wisconsin, on 1 October 1901. He was left with three children and the homestead. A third child, Raymond, is named at John's death in 1934, though the 1906 notice gives no names.

John kept the family together. He farmed the old Frisch place on Oak Ridge until about 1929, then moved to Rollingstone, where he served as secretary of the Rollingstone Mutual Farmers Fire Insurance Company for twenty-four years and in 1932 as president of the state association of mutual insurance companies. He remarried in 1931, to Mrs. Anna Breitbach of Winona. Viola married Edward Rivers in June 1933, and John died on 16 March 1934 of an acute heart attack, 'while members of his family were at his bedside.' Edward N. Rivers began as an insurance agent at Rollingstone that same year.

A parent left alone with young children recurs in this family. John did it on Oak Ridge in 1906, and across the river in Wisconsin in 1977 the same shape came round again when Viola's daughter Diane was left with five. The Frisch farm had two funerals in three weeks, and the girl who was sixteen months old grew up to marry the insurance agent in the next village.

stories.title: The town the railroad missed
stories.hook: In 1872 the Houston and Texas Central laid its tracks two miles east of Mantua, Texas. By the middle of 1873 the town was deserted, and the Williams, Parker and Bell families ended up in the places that replaced it.
body: Mantua was founded in 1854 to pay for a school. Three men bought 200 acres from a son of Collin McKinney, cut it into lots and sold them to fund Mantua Seminary. The town banned gambling, horse racing and the sale of liquor, "to insure the proper environment" for the students. By 1860 it had three stores, a church and about fifty people, and by 1870 about 300.

Then the Houston and Texas Central Railway laid its tracks two miles east. Some Mantua citizens bought land by the line and started a new town, Van Alstyne, in Grayson County. The post office closed on 11 July 1873, and by mid-1873 Mantua was deserted except for the churches, which moved in 1888. Van Alstyne incorporated in 1890 with about 400 people, two gristmills, a flour mill, a newspaper and a college, and had about 1,940 residents around 1900.

Anna, five miles southeast of old Mantua, came a decade later: platted in 1883 with twenty people, two stores, a steam gristmill and a Baptist church, with 100 to 200 people by 1890, a first bank in 1902 and incorporation in 1913. The population was 538 in 1929, 467 in 1931. A traction line, the Greenville and Northwestern, ran from Anna to Blue Ridge from about 1915 to 1920.

The living came from the land. Collin County had 903 farms in 1870 and 6,001 in 1920, when it grew 49,311 bales of cotton and nearly 2.6 million bushels of corn. Grayson County's farms peaked at 5,762 in 1900. In the Depression Collin County lost more than 1,200 farms between 1930 and 1940, and Grayson County nearly 900.

Rachel's families sit within a few miles of the dead town. Thomas and Rebecca Williams brought their sons from Tennessee about 1891, to the Mantua country, and a youngest son, George, was born there that year. The Parkers' deaths, in the tree, are at Monta and Van Alstyne. Wayne Bell was born at Anna in 1914. He married Melba Williams at Van Alstyne in 1937, and the two of them farmed Grayson County for the rest of their working lives. The Williams and Parker graves are at Van Alstyne, in the town the railroad built.

stories.title: Raford Failes, sixty, in Milam County
stories.hook: In 1870 a census taker in Milam County, Texas, wrote down Raford Failes, a North Carolina native of sixty with a little Mississippi-born daughter. The Fails had come west after the Civil War.
body: The 1870 census taker in Milam County wrote down "Raford Failes," sixty, born in North Carolina, as head of a household (page 212, line 19), and in the same house a seven-year-old, "Elizabeth Failes," born in Mississippi. It was five years after the Civil War. Milam County, east of Austin, had seen its farm values fall by more than half between 1860 and 1870, from about $1.14 million to $505,000, and recovery was slow, the Handbook of Texas says, because transportation was poor and everyone lived off the land. Complete recovery waited for the railroads of the 1870s.

Rayford Fail was born on 16 March 1806, probably in Johnston County, North Carolina, and married Polly Anne Wallace by 1838. Their children were born in Jasper County, Mississippi: George Washington in August 1847, Young Rayford in December 1853, Jeremiah Marsh in March 1854, Thomas in February 1857 and Temperence Elizabeth in February 1863. Because Temperence was born in Mississippi in 1863 and the family was in Texas by mid-1870, the move west came in those seven years, during or just after the war. Rayford died in Milam County on 26 January 1885.

His children made Milam County theirs. George Washington Fail married Margaret Ann Johnson there in 1870 and died in the county in 1923. Young Rayford married Viney Allison in 1873, had three sons, and died on 6 September 1880. Temperence, called Lizzie, married Joseph Franklin Keen in Lee County on 7 March 1878.

The Keens went on to Lamar County, Texas, and soon after the 1900 census into the Choctaw Nation. In 1910 "Lizzie Keen," fifty-nine, a widow, was head of a household at Oakes, Choctaw County, Oklahoma, the same township where Joel Anderson Johnson and Winnie were living. She was buried at Forest Chapel Cemetery in Lamar County, and the Southeast Oklahoman of Hugo noted her death on 14 December 1939. Other Fail descendants, Thomas Fail (died 1936) and Jim "Tobe" Fail (died 1957), ended up in Choctaw County or Greer County, Oklahoma. It was the same road Joel Anderson's family took, a generation later: out of Mississippi to Texas, then over the Red River.

What is not proved is the link to the Johnsons. Joel Anderson Johnson was born in Milam County in April 1875, and his census returns give a mother born in Mississippi. That fits a Fail, but no record names her. The tree's Marjorie Rebecca Fail, born at Turnersville, Jasper County, in 1849, would be a daughter of Rayford, yet she is not on the published Fail lists. The tree's George Washington Johnson may also have blended two men: Rayford's son George Washington Fail married a Margaret Ann Johnson in Milam County in 1870.

stories.title: Anna Brose Nelton and twenty-one years of illness
stories.hook: Anna Nelton died on a Sunday evening in April 1928 at forty-four, and her husband told the newspaper where he thought it had started: a rattlesnake bite in June 1907.
body: Anna Louise (Brose) Nelton lived with a long illness while raising four children in Winona. Her husband George associated the beginning of that illness with a rattlesnake bite “across the lake” in June 1907. The family’s account was published after her death, but it supplies no medical diagnosis or treatment history. The bite and the cause of the continuing illness cannot be medically confirmed from that account.

Anna died at the family home on West Broadway on the evening of 8 April 1928, aged forty-four. The family described twenty-one years of illness, reaching back to 1907. Her youngest child Arthur was born in October 1909 and was eighteen when she died. The long span is part of her life story, while the exact nature of her condition remains unknown.

She had been born Anna Louise Brose in Winona on 26 December 1883, to Ernest and Augusta Brose, German immigrants, and "spent all her life here." She married George, then a house carpenter, and by 1910 had four children: Myrtle, Irwin, Edward and Arthur. The family rented at 617 West King Street that spring, and later lived on West Broadway.

She left her husband and the four children, with Myrtle still at home and unmarried, two brothers, Ernest and John Brose, and three sisters, Minnie Brose, Mrs. Max Schulze and Mrs. Niels Skow. The funeral was held at the house and then at McKinley Methodist Church, with burial at Woodlawn Cemetery. Arthur was eighteen. A little more than two years later George married again.

stories.title: Ernest and Augusta Brose and their six Winona children
stories.hook: Two Germans from Posen reached Winona by 1883, raised six children there, and left behind a railroad yardmaster, a World War I veteran and a family lot at Woodlawn.
body: Ernest Brose, born in May 1847, and Augusta, born in December 1856, came from Germany to Winona before the birth of their daughter Anna in December 1883. Their reported place of origin is Wolwark near Schubin, in the Bromberg district of the former Prussian province of Posen. That precise origin remains to be confirmed. The family’s documented American life centered on Winona.

The town they reached had been drawing Germans since 1856 on the strength of its lumber, wheat, steamboats and railroads; the first railroad out of Winona had opened in 1862. Six of their children grew to adulthood, all born in Winona: Anna (1883), Ida (1885), Louise (8 December 1886), Ernest Gustav (23 December 1890), Minnie (27 June 1893) and John H. (1 July 1895).

Augusta died on 28 April 1924, aged sixty-seven. Ernest lived ten more years and died in Winona on 4 September 1934, aged eighty-seven. Both are buried at Woodlawn Cemetery, Section AA, Lot 66, where their son John also lies.

The children made their lives in Winona. Ida married Niels Petersen Skow in 1922 and died in 1946. Louise married Max E. Schulze on 2 January 1911 and "lived in Winona most of her life." Anna married the carpenter George Nelton. Ernest Gustav became a yardmaster for the Northwestern Railway, retired in September 1948 and in 1949 married Lydia Zambrocki at St. Casimir's Church; as a veteran of the First World War he died at the Minneapolis Veterans Hospital on 1 June 1965 and was buried at St. Mary's Cemetery. Minnie married William Julius Schellhas and died in 1971 in Winona, the last of the six.

The siblings’ lives crossed several Winona institutions. Anna’s funeral was held at McKinley Methodist Church, Louise’s at Grace Presbyterian, and Ernest Gustav married at St. Casimir’s Catholic Church. Building work, the railway and these congregations placed the family within different parts of the same river city.

stories.title: Eda Zenk Nelton and her six children
stories.hook: Eda Nelton, born in Germany in 1852, was a widow for thirty-two years, saw her son become a Winona contractor, and died at ninety-one in the last week of 1943.
body: Eda Ida Zenk Nelton died in Winona on 30 December 1943, at ninety-one, in the third winter of the United States' war with the country she was born in. She was buried at Woodlawn Cemetery. She had been born in Germany on 15 March 1852. Her birthplace is given as Pommern, a village on the Mosel in the Rhineland, though 'Pommern' is also the German name of Pomerania, and which was meant is unsettled.

Her husband, George Nelton, born in January 1855, is the family's other unsolved German. He is said to have died on 19 October 1911. The surname itself is unexplained; the original form may have been Nölte, Nelte or something similar. What is certain is that by early 1882 the two of them were in Winona, because their son George John was born there on 17 January of that year.

She is credited with six children, all born in Winona: Anna (1879, later Mrs. Joseph Knopp, married 1899, died 1974); George John (17 January 1882, the contractor); Winifred, called Winnie (4 March 1882, Mrs. Arthur Oscar Beeman, died 1966); Edith Thelma (17 September 1888, Mrs. Eaton, died at La Crosse in 1962); Harry (1892-1966); and Elsie (29 January 1896, Mrs. Victor Z. Bitu, died 1968). Two of those dates cannot both be right: George and Winnie are listed as born only seven weeks apart in 1882. One date is wrong, or one of them was not Eda's child. Elsie's eldest son, Jenus Arvid Bitu, died in 1927 at thirteen.

The son whose life is best documented is George John, who built houses around Winona. His second wife was Christine Walstad, a Norwegian born on 3 December 1888, who came to America in 1904 and married him in 1930. She worked at the Williams Hotel Cafeteria, Winona Cleaning Works and Miller Waste Mills, and became a United States citizen in September 1941. George's surviving children were sons Irwin, Arthur and Edward and daughter Mrs. Andrew (Myrtle) Wally.

A Mrs. Charles Nelton of Winona was badly hurt in January 1913 when her horse bolted in front of a Chicago Great Western train, and a Charles Nelton (1880-1963) lived in Winona with his wife Rose. Neither is a known child of Eda, and no document connects them to this family.

stories.title: Jacob Johns of Hart Township: from Baltimore to Fort Blakely
stories.hook: At twenty Jacob Johns left a Winona County farm for the Sixth Minnesota Infantry, and ended up in the swamps of Arkansas and the last siege of the Civil War; he later fathered twelve children, one of whom married into the Rivers family.
body: Jacob Johns of Hart Township enlisted in Company E of the Sixth Minnesota Infantry on 15 August 1862. His 1895 biography gives his birth as 5 August 1842 in Germany, making him twenty at enlistment; the family tree instead gives 1840. He arrived in America as a young child after a two-month voyage to Baltimore. The family spent seven years in Missouri, moved to Hazel Green, Wisconsin, and settled in Hart Township in 1856.

His service included the battles of Birch Coulee on 2 September 1862 and Wood Lake on 23 September during the U.S.–Dakota War. The conflict brought severe losses and displacement to Dakota communities as well as deaths among soldiers and settlers. That December, thirty-eight Dakota men were executed at Mankato. The Sixth Minnesota remained on the frontier and took part in military expeditions into Dakota territory in 1863.

In June 1864 the Sixth Minnesota was sent to Helena, Arkansas, where disease devastated the regiment. By late September, 654 of its 950 men were reported sick, mostly with malaria. Jacob later served in the Mobile campaign at Spanish Fort and Fort Blakely in 1865. He completed his service as a private, without being wounded or taken prisoner, and was discharged on 19 August 1865.

He bought eighty acres in section 28 of Hart Township, which grew to 440. On 18 May 1868 he married Theresa (the book prints her surname as "Kryzer"). The twelve children were Mary, Sophia, Lizzie, Emma, Annie, Jacob, Henry, Rose, Willie, Hannah, Eddie and George. The family was Catholic, Jacob was a Democrat, and he served as township supervisor and constable and belonged to the Grand Army of the Republic.

Johanna Johns, who married Edward Rivers Sr. of Rollingstone on 22 June 1909, was born on 11 November 1888 at Rushford in Fillmore County, 'to Jacob and Theresa Johns.' She died at home in Rollingstone on 4 March 1967 and was buried at Holy Trinity Catholic Cemetery. She was survived by a brother, George, in Canada and a sister, Mrs. Rose Tiernan, in Albertville. Johanna is probably the Hannah of the 1895 list of children; the link rests on the parents' names, the sibling names and the location, and is not proven. Her marriage joined a German Catholic farm family to the Luxembourg Catholic Riverses, and both her father and her husband's uncle, John B. Rivers of the 48th Wisconsin, had worn Union blue.

The connection to Johanna has more than names behind it. The 1895 household contained seven daughters and five sons, including Hannah, Rose and George. Johanna's 1967 family notice names Rose and George as her surviving siblings and records five sisters and four brothers who had already died. Those counts fit the earlier household exactly. Together with Jacob and Theresa's names and the Rushford area, they make Hannah's identification as Johanna a strong possibility, though an original birth or marriage record is still needed to settle it.

stories.title: Wings in August, a parade in January
stories.hook: Two hometown newspaper items follow Bob Johnson from jump school in 1958 to the Kennedy inaugural parade in 1961.
body: In August 1958 Bob Johnson earned his parachutist wings at the 82nd Airborne Division Jump School at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. The course included five training jumps. He was twenty-one and only six months into his Army service, having entered that February and completed basic training at Fort Ord, California.

Before the Army, Bob attended Decatur Baptist College in Texas. His parents lived in different communities: his father Joel G. Johnson remained on the Boehler Route near Boswell, while his mother Nettie was then Mrs. Nettie B. McCarter of Sherman. Those family addresses accompanied the announcement of his airborne qualification.

Jump school at Fort Bragg was the gate to the Army's airborne divisions. The 82nd Airborne, headquartered there, was a Strategic Army Corps unit, which the Army described as ready to deploy anywhere on short notice.

By January 1961 Bob was a Specialist Four and a supply clerk in the Mortar Battery of the 504th Infantry, 82nd Airborne Division. He had served in Germany and was again based at Fort Bragg. That month he marched with his unit in President John F. Kennedy’s inaugural parade in Washington. At twenty-three, the 1957 Decatur High School graduate had already served on both sides of the Atlantic.

His mother's name changed in the three years between the items. In 1958 she is Mrs. Nettie B. McCarter of Route 2, Sherman; in 1961, Mrs. Nettie B. Tillery of Sadler, Texas. She had been Nettie Tyson, and the household she grew up in is told in the story of the two Tyson sisters. She died on 6 February 1980 and is buried at Sunnyside Cemetery in Savoy, Fannin County, Texas, her last residence.

These were the Army's own hometown releases, mailed from Fort Bragg to the papers in a soldier's home county, and the earliest published notice of a career that would run twenty years through Germany, Korea and Vietnam and end with a Warrant Officer 3's rank. Eleven months after the parade, on 21 December 1961, he married Margie Bell.

stories.title: A license in July 1938
stories.hook: The Choctaw County court docket records Opal Tyson's marriage license, the first step toward the Wilson, Johnson and Tyson household of 1940.
body: In July 1938 Opal Tyson and Seidel Wilson obtained a marriage license in Choctaw County, Oklahoma. The couple appeared among the Boswell marriage-license notices published that month in the Paris News and the Southeast Oklahoman. Opal was eighteen. A license documents the intention to marry; the notices do not supply a ceremony date.

By the spring of 1940 she was living as Opal Wilson at her father Albert Tyson’s rented farm in Oakes Township. With her was her infant son Don. Her sister Nettie Johnson and Nettie’s young son Bob were in the same household, alongside their parents and younger brother Marion.

Over the following decade, the children’s households changed. In 1950 Opal was enumerated as Joe Johnson’s wife, with Don as Joe’s stepson and Bob living with them. A later marriage between Opal Wilson and Joel Gilbert Johnson was recorded in Sevier County, Arkansas, on 3 December 1968. The earlier household and later marriage record are distinct events; they do not establish when the couple first began living together.

stories.title: The Rivers store and the families around it
stories.hook: John B. Rivers opened a Rollingstone store in 1872. His children carried on its trade, linking the Rivers, Heber and Jung families.
body: John B. Rivers, Henry Rivers’s brother, married Anna Heber on 29 October 1866, the same year he bought a farm in Norton Township. He opened a store in Rollingstone in 1872. Their children were John H., Matthew, John P., Elizabeth and Josephine. Anna’s father was Nicholas Heber.

John H. Rivers, born in Norton Township on 13 December 1867, studied at Winona State Normal School and a Winona business college before working with his father. He later ran a grocery in Winona with his brother John P. In 1896 he returned to Rollingstone and opened a general dry goods business. His brother Matthew, born at Rollingstone on 8 December 1874, stayed in the family general store and served as assistant postmaster. The brothers carried their father's work into a new generation.

John H. married Bertha Jung on 10 October 1894. Her parents, merchant John Jung and Margaretha Kohner, belonged to Rollingstone's 1855 settlers. Their children Andrew and Angeline were born on 10 December 1895 and 13 October 1899. The marriage linked two village business families, while their cousins continued the Rivers mail route.

Arthur Nelton marries Helen Canfield in Winona on 15 August.
Wayne Bell marries Melba Williams at Van Alstyne, Texas, on 18 September.
Bobby Joe Johnson is born at Buckhorn, Oklahoma, on 17 July.
David John Nelton is born in Winona on 19 July.
Diane Mary Rivers is born in St. Paul on 10 August.
Joe Johnson and Wayne Bell both register for the draft on 16 October.
Joe Johnson enlists; he serves with the 872nd Engineer Aviation Battalion until October 1945.
David Nelton and Diane Rivers marry at Holy Trinity Church, Rollingstone, on 26 July.
Joe Johnson dies of a heart attack at his home near Boswell on 25 November.
Diane Nelton files a sex-discrimination complaint against her La Crosse employer.
David Nelton dies after a head-on collision on Highway 53, La Crosse, on 12 February.
Melba Bell dies at home in Denison, Texas, on 22 September.
Arthur Nelton dies at La Crosse on 7 October; his grandsons are pallbearers.
Diane (Rivers) Antony dies of cancer at La Crosse on 27 March, aged forty-seven.

Michel and Margaret Rivers leave Luxembourg; they settle on a Winona County farm the next year.
Jacques and Anna Frisch land at Winona on the Fourth of July and settle at Oak Ridge.
Joel Anderson Johnson is born in Milam County, Texas, on 2 April.
Joel A. Johnson marries Winnie Bozarth in Texas.
Edward Rivers Sr. starts the new rural mail route out of Rollingstone; he carries it for thirty years.
Maggie Frisch dies at Oak Ridge two weeks after giving birth; her father-in-law Jacob dies nineteen days later.
George Nelton spends the winter contracting in Florida during the land boom.
The census finds Nettie Johnson and two-year-old Bob living with her parents, the Tysons, at Oakes.
George Nelton, Winona contractor, dies on 12 November.
Joel Anderson Johnson dies at Hugo, aged eighty-five.
Diane Nelton marries Stephen Fascher on 28 May; he dies on 7 August 1978, aged thirty-one.
Wayne and Melba Bell's infant son is born prematurely at Sherman on 9 April and lives seven hours.
David Glenn Johnson is born in Christian County, Kentucky, near Fort Campbell, on 8 July.
David Glenn Johnson, 24, dies after a pickup rollover east of Atoka on 20 October.
Anna (Brose) Nelton dies in Winona on 8 April, when her son Arthur is eighteen.
Helen (Canfield) Nelton dies at home in Minnesota City on 30 November.
Rayford Fail's household is enumerated in Milam County, Texas
Temperence Fail marries Joseph Franklin Keen in Lee County, Texas
Jacob Johns of Hart Township enlists in Company E, Sixth Minnesota Infantry (Birch Coulee, 2 Sept.).
Anna Nelton bitten by a rattlesnake in June, an injury her husband later tied to her 21-year illness.

Ernest Brose dies in Winona, aged 87 (4 Sept.).
Marjorie Ann "Margie" Bell is born in Texas on 16 March.
Bob Johnson and Margie Bell marry on 21 December, the start of twenty years of Army life.
Margie Johnson dies at Calera, Oklahoma, on 12 February, five months after Bob.

John B. Rivers marries Anna Heber and buys a Norton Township farm.
John B. Rivers opens his store in Rollingstone.
John H. Rivers marries Bertha Jung, joining two Rollingstone merchant families.
John H. Rivers returns to Rollingstone and opens a dry goods business.
